strengths: The manuscript studies a practically relevant and underexplored relationship among diffusion seeds, generated samples, and approximate DDIM inversions.
The experiments span pixel-space and latent diffusion models on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and CelebA, with useful timestep sweeps, multiple training checkpoints, and generally clear visualizations.
The asymmetric nearest-neighbor matching result and the apparent early stabilization of same-seed image content are interesting empirical observations worthy of further investigation.
The presentation is organized and engages with recent work on inversion, consistency, and optimal-transport interpretations.
weaknesses: The evidence that inverted latents are not standard Gaussian is inadequate. Selecting the top ten correlations among millions of coordinate pairs creates a strong multiple-comparison effect, as demonstrated by the surprisingly large correlations already obtained for true Gaussian noise. The paper omits a matched LDM noise baseline and does not examine means, variances, covariance spectra, marginal normality, or calibrated distributional tests.

The central training-time inversion conclusion is confounded: Figure 4 inverts samples produced by the final model using intermediate checkpoints. This mismatches the generator and inverter and cannot establish whether inversion quality for each checkpoint's own samples improves during training.

The claim that an inverted latent lies along the sampling trajectory is stronger than the evidence. Triangle angles and proximity to an interpolation segment do not establish membership in the nonlinear trajectory; normalized errors, uncertainty, null comparisons, and comparisons with exact or improved inversion methods are missing.

Nearest-neighbor assignment under raw Euclidean distance is highly sensitive to vector norms, scaling, and dimensional concentration. The reverse-direction failures are themselves dominated by low-variance images. Results with normalization, whitening, cosine distance, controlled synthetic baselines, and different candidate-set sizes are needed before concluding that L2 defines the noise-image mapping.

The claim that only high-frequency details improve later in training is not supported by a frequency-resolved analysis. CKA, SVCCA, SSIM, DINO similarity, and the KNN-coverage statistic are insufficiently defined and do not isolate spatial frequencies or semantic stability.

The scope is limited to low-resolution unconditional models and generated images. There are no modern text-conditioned models, classifier-free guidance settings, real-image inversions, downstream editing experiments, or baselines such as ReNoise and exact/fixed-point inversion, limiting practical significance.

Reproducibility is weak: exact architectures and checkpoints, preprocessing and value ranges, LDM representation details, metric implementations, uncertainty calculations, and code are not provided. The stated DDIM variance formula also appears to omit the standard square root.

Several findings are closely related to already cited observations about imperfect DDIM inversion, optimal transport, and cross-model seed consistency. Without stronger controls, theory, or a demonstrated application, the remaining contribution is primarily descriptive and not yet competitive for a top-tier venue.

The empirical scope is substantial: six diffusion models spanning pixel and latent spaces, multiple datasets and architectures, large sample counts, and inversion schedules from 50 to 1000 steps.

Per-timestep error and variance analyses, followed by targeted replacement of early inversion steps, provide useful mechanistic evidence. The proposed intervention is simple, inexpensive, and often improves latent normality and downstream metrics.
The paper is generally clear and includes interpolation, editing, reconstruction, speed, ablation, and qualitative real-image results, alongside limitations, compute, and broader-impact discussions.
weaknesses: The central plain-versus-non-plain error analysis is potentially confounded: Equations 13–14 sum masked errors without normalizing by the number of selected pixels, despite the results being described as per-pixel. Important measurements are insufficiently specified, including how the top-20 Pearson correlations and KL divergence are estimated and aggregated. Most downstream results lack uncertainty or significance analysis.

The editing evaluation treats greater distance from the source and lower source-prompt alignment as improvement, but does not adequately measure preservation of unedited content, localized edit fidelity, or human preference. Most quantitative experiments use model-generated inputs and disable classifier-free guidance; real-image evidence is only qualitative.

Baseline coverage is incomplete for the broad claims: closely related noise-schedule, exact-inversion, edit-friendly DDPM, and modern editing approaches are not compared on the same downstream tasks. Meanwhile, the 4% method worsens SDXL reconstruction from LPIPS 0.10 to 0.14 and PSNR 27.58 to 25.68, making the claim of negligible degradation too strong.

Nearly all quantitative experiments use images generated by the same model, where the original Gaussian noise is known, and classifier-free guidance is disabled. This is substantially easier than practical inversion of real, out-of-distribution images under normal guidance. Real-image evidence consists only of four qualitative examples, so the main practical editing claim is insufficiently supported.

Novelty is limited: prior work already identifies non-Gaussian DDIM inversions and large early-time numerical errors, while injecting forward noise is closely related to established stochastic editing ideas. Missing comparisons include stronger exact or edit-oriented inversion methods and relevant scheduling/forward-noising baselines. The paper evaluates only a small subset of cited alternatives yet broadly concludes that prior inversion methods do not solve the problem.

The mechanism is not adequately isolated. There is no matched-energy random perturbation, final-latent whitening/rescaling, or early-versus-middle-versus-late replacement control. Thus the improvements may simply reflect adding randomness and forgetting the source, rather than specifically correcting the diagnosed correlations.

Important implementation and metric details are underspecified, including the Pearson-correlation and KL estimators, some sample counts, mask transfer to latent resolutions, checkpoint/configuration details, and baseline hyperparameters. Algorithm 1 also gives a DDIM coefficient inconsistent with Equation 5, and the claimed code link is rendered only as a dangling "a" with no usable URL.

The interpolation experiments evaluate marginal sample quality with FID/precision/recall but do not establish semantic path smoothness, endpoint fidelity, or perceptual transition quality. The empirical investigation is broad, covering conditional and unconditional models, pixel- and latent-space architectures, several resolutions, and inversion lengths up to 1,000 steps.

Replacing the earliest inversion steps with forward diffusion is simple, computationally inexpensive, and produces substantial improvements in the reported correlation, KL-divergence, interpolation, and prompt-alignment measurements.

The paper reports reasonably large sample sizes, comparisons with several inversion methods, qualitative results, pseudocode, failure cases, computational costs, limitations, and broader-impact considerations.
weaknesses: The central claim that inversion errors are larger specifically in plain regions is not rigorously established. Equations 13–14 sum errors within each mask but do not divide by the number of selected pixels, so differences between plain and non-plain regions can be driven by mask area. The treatment of image-space masks for lower-resolution latent grids and sensitivity to the fixed threshold are also unspecified.

The editing evaluation conflates editability with destruction of source information. The method explicitly injects fresh noise, while the reported diversity metrics reward distance from the source and the CLIP metrics reward movement toward randomly paired target prompts. Reconstruction also degrades—for example, Table 7 changes LPIPS from 0.10 to 0.14 and PSNR from 27.58 to 25.68—yet results are not compared at matched source fidelity. Quantitative evaluation on a standard real-image editing benchmark or human assessment is missing.

The claimed Gaussianity is stronger than the evidence supports. Local pairwise correlations and an insufficiently defined KL estimate do not establish multivariate normality or absence of semantic dependence; moreover, decorrelation is partly expected mechanically when Gaussian noise is injected.

The methodological novelty is limited, and the relationship to forward-noising or SDEdit-style stochastic editing is not adequately isolated. A matched baseline that injects the same amount of noise without the remaining inversion procedure would be essential, as would comparisons against stronger contemporary editing/inversion pipelines at equivalent reconstruction quality.

Practical generality remains uncertain: conditional experiments disable classifier-free guidance, most quantitative analyses use model-generated rather than real images, and the replacement parameter is expressed as a percentage of solver steps even though the appropriate amount depends on the noise schedule and SNR. No principled rule for selecting it is provided.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The advertised code link is broken or absent, and important details—including correlation/KL computation, mask resizing, baseline configurations, interpolation reference distributions, checkpoint identifiers, and uncertainty for several principal results—are missing. Overall, the empirical phenomenon is promising, but these soundness and evaluation gaps place the work marginally below the acceptance threshold.
